Planes at Sofia airport. Two Ryanair flights from Copenhagen and Madrid made emergency landings in the Bulgarian capital. Photograph: Stoyan Nenov/Reuters

Bomb threats disrupt dozens of flights across Europe, raising hybrid war fears

Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel

• Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

Hoax bomb threats have disrupted at least 34 flights across Europe this week, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

At least 25 bomb threats affected flights on Thursday between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.

The threats affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious.

In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.

The Met said threats had been made against four aircraft departing from or arriving at Heathrow. A police spokesperson added that, after an assessment, “no security issues [were] identified”.

Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

Read more

The day of hoaxes followed similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance.

Investigators said on Thursday there remained no evidence that the hoaxes were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, although inquiries across Europe into the incidents continue.

Map of Europe showing routes of flights reportedly subject to bomb threats and diverted flights

The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma, which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse.

Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov. On his Telegram channel Pozdnyakov, a prominent supporter of the war in Ukraine, did not comment on or claim responsibility for the bomb threats.

The emails reportedly read: “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this for ever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”

A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the airport had received an anonymous threat by phone on Thursday morning, causing a flight to be delayed. It was understood to be a Ryanair flight from London Stansted.

A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels-Charleroi was inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard toilet.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.

Malpensa airport in Milan, where a Ryanair flight was searched after landing. Photograph: Claudia Greco/Reuters

The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems.

Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?

Read more

A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

In Rome, Guido Crosetto, the Italian defence minister, said: “It seems to me that every day now, from refrigerators to blood supplies in France, to these fake alarms, there’s someone who has an interest in stoking tensions.”

Asked if he knew who was behind the hoaxes, he said: “It’s called ‘under-threshold warfare’ because it’s below the attribution threshold. It’s done that way on purpose, so no one can pin the blame.”

Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.

A police officer and sniffer dog inspecting a Ryanair plane and baggage in Murcia, Spain on Tuesday. Photograph: Forta/Reuters

Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.

While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.

A LOT Polish Airlines passenger aircraft takes off from Brussels airport after undergoing security checks. Photograph: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/Getty Images

Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.

He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.

items.summary: 据卫报报道，英国央行三年多来首次加息，将基准利率从3.75%上调至4%，货币政策委员会八名成员投票支持，一名成员主张加息半个百分点。央行预计明年年中英国通胀率将升至4.9%，高于7月预测的3.2%。行长贝利表示，除非中东冲突得到解决，否则这不太可能是最后一次加息。下次利率决定将于12月17日公布。

Before the Iran war the Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee had been expected to cut interest rates this year. Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

Before the Iran war the Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee had been expected to cut interest rates this year. Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, the first increase for more than three years

Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation

• Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.

Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.

The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices persistently above $100 a barrel in recent months, as hopes have evaporated of a deal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz.

As a result, the Bank now expects UK inflation to rise to 4.9% in the middle of next year – up from 3.2% in its last economic forecast in July. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, as measured on the consumer prices index.

The decision, which will hit mortgage borrowers, comes a week after John Healey used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers. Echoing the Office for Budget Responsibility’s gloomy forecasts for living standards, the MPC expects real post-tax income to fall this year and next.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, raised the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

“Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach,” he said, according to the MPC minutes.

A graph showing UK interest rates from before 2007 to 2026

However, he played down the likelihood of a prolonged series of increases, as markets have been predicting. “Today’s increase shouldn’t be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence in hikes. But unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase,” he said.

The Bank’s next interest rate decision will be announced on 17 December, and some analysts suggested the MPC could press ahead with a pre-Christmas hike.

Andrew Goodwin, the chief economist at consultancy Oxford Economics, said: “The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike in December or February is likely.”

Explaining its decision to raise borrowing costs, the MPC highlighted the pass-through from elevated oil prices to business and consumer costs across the economy. It expects the Ofgem energy cap to rise from the equivalent of £1,723 a year for an average household in Great Britain to £2,150 in January and to increase again in April. Food price inflation could hit 4.75% by mid-2027, it warned.

The head of France's CGT labour union, Sophie Binet (C), said the wave of protests and strikes had reached a new level

ByPaul Kirby

Europe digital editor

More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.

The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.

As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.

The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.

The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.

Some unrest was reported in several cities.

A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.

Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.

The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.

Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise Léon, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A car was set alight during a protest in the centre of Lyon

A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic, which is currently €12.31 (£10) an hour.

Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.

An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.

Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.

Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.

Image source, Philippe LOPEZ / AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Disruption was already reported at schools on Thursday morning

The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of €100 a month," Marylise Léon explained.

The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.

The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".

However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.

The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike on Thursday, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycées, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.

"Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.

Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.

• France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at policePublished2 November

Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the Élysée Palace, and the prime minister's residence at Hôtel Matignon.

Instead, the march followed another central route from Place de la République to Place de la Nation.

The interior minister had earlier spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

Demonstrators demanded debt relief for poorer countries at the IMF-World Bank annual summit in Bangkok in October. Photograph: Peerapon Boonyakiat/Sopa Images/Shutterstock

Debt of poorest countries at record $9.4tn high, World Bank data shows

Cost of servicing external debt is preventing developing countries from investing for future

Debt owed by developing countries rose to a record $9.4tn (£7tn) last year, with the poorest paying the highest interest rates since the late 1980s, World Bank data shows.

The UK government is preparing to champion a “new drive on debt” as part of its presidency of the G20 next year – a move the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has linked to confronting the legacy of slavery.

In its annual International Debt Report, the World Bank said the rising cost of servicing external debt was preventing some governments from investing for the future.

The increase in developing country debt last year, of 5.5%, was the fastest in four years, the report finds – driven by a rapid rise in private sector lending.

The World Bank’s chief statistician, Haishan Fu, said: “Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.”

On average, the report found the poorest countries – those eligible for concessional lending from the World Bank – faced an average interest rate of 8.2% on new borrowing: the highest since the late 1980s. It also said preliminary data for 2026 suggested lending continued at a rapid pace – but at continued high interest rates as global financing costs rose.

The Bank highlighted recent borrowing by Laos, at an interest rate of 11.5%, the Republic of Congo, at 13.88%, and Kenya, at 9.2%.

Analysing the connection between a high debt burden and the ability to spend on domestic priorities, the World Bank found global shocks had more impact on the availability of food in heavily indebted countries.

“Food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress,” the report said.

Burnham has appointed the former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown to examine the feasibility of changes to the global debt regime in the run-up to the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, set out plans last month for a “new deal” for heavily indebted countries in a speech at the IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. The deal is likely to include proposals to mobilise the balance sheets of the World Bank and other multilateral development banks to buy back outstanding debt in an effort to extend repayment periods and bring down interest rates.

However, the situation is more complex than in the run-up to the Gleneagles summit in 2005 – when G8 countries signed up to write off billions of pounds worth of debt – because today’s creditors tend to be private-sector bondholders, not governments.

There have been growing demands in recent years for changes to the framework for international debt, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa.
